blocks.text: A local minimum is a point where a function value is lower than every point immediately nearby, without necessarily being the lowest point the function can reach anywhere. Gradient descent can settle into one and stop, even when a better minimum exists somewhere else entirely on the same surface.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733787-714969312.png
1. What a Local Minimum Is

A local minimum is a point where the function value is lower than at every point in its immediate neighborhood. Moving a small distance in any direction from a local minimum only increases the function value, at least locally.

code.content:
import numpy as np
def f(x):
    return x**4 - 4*x**2 + x   # has two local minima
xs = np.linspace(-3, 3, 500)
ys = f(xs)
print(xs[np.argmin(ys)])   # the global minimum, but a second local minimum also exists nearby

blocks.text: This local-only view is exactly the limitation every gradient based method shares, they optimize by feel, following the immediate slope, with no global map of the entire surface.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: For the function x squared, every point except x equals 0 has a higher value than at least one nearby point closer to 0, meaning x equals 0 is the only local minimum, and it also happens to be the global one.

blocks.text: The term local is doing precise mathematical work here, it means the comparison is only made against nearby points, never against the function value everywhere else in its domain.

Recognizing that a point is only a local minimum, not necessarily the best one available, is the first step toward understanding why so many optimization techniques exist beyond plain gradient descent.
2. Local Versus Global Minima

A function can have many local minima, but among all of them, at most one, or a tied set, qualifies as the global minimum, the single lowest value the function reaches anywhere in its domain. Every global minimum is automatically a local minimum, but not every local minimum is global.

Identifying every local minimum of a complicated function analytically is often infeasible, which is why practical optimization instead relies on techniques like random restarts and momentum rather than an exhaustive search.
When multiple local minima happen to share the exact same lowest value, they are all simultaneously considered global minima, a tie rather than a single unique point.
This tie situation is more common than it might seem, many functions built from repeating or symmetric patterns naturally produce several equally good minima.
3. Why Gradient Descent Can Get Stuck

Gradient descent only ever looks at the local slope at the current position, it has no way of knowing whether a better minimum exists further away. Once it reaches a point where the gradient is zero and the surface curves upward in every direction, it stops, regardless of whether that point is the best possible minimum.

code.content:
def gradient_descent_1d(start, learning_rate, steps, grad_fn):
    x = start
    for _ in range(steps):
        x = x - learning_rate * grad_fn(x)
    return x

grad = lambda x: 4*x**3 - 8*x + 1
print(gradient_descent_1d(-2.5, 0.01, 200, grad))   # settles into whichever local minimum is nearest the start

blocks.text: This is a direct, unavoidable consequence of how gradient descent is defined, it has no mechanism for looking beyond the immediate neighborhood of its current position.

This blindness to the broader shape of the function is the price paid for gradient descent efficiency, it never needs to examine the entire surface, only the small region immediately around its current position.
This is not a flaw specific to gradient descent, it is a fundamental limitation of any purely local, slope-following search method applied to a non-convex surface.
Understanding this limitation clearly is what motivates the escape techniques covered later in this lesson, since the limitation itself cannot be removed, only worked around.
4. Starting Point Matters

Because gradient descent only follows the local slope, where it starts strongly influences which local minimum it ends up in. Two different starting points on the same function can converge to two entirely different local minima.

code.content:
print(gradient_descent_1d(-2.5, 0.01, 200, grad))   # one local minimum
print(gradient_descent_1d(2.5, 0.01, 200, grad))    # possibly a different one

blocks.text: This sensitivity to starting point is exactly why neural network weights are initialized randomly, giving each individual training run a different starting position and therefore a chance at finding a different, possibly better, minimum.

Training the same neural network architecture multiple times from different random initializations, then keeping the best resulting model, is a direct, practical application of this starting-point sensitivity.
Some training setups deliberately try several different random seeds and keep the model that performs best on a validation set, directly accounting for this starting point sensitivity.
5. Saddle Points

A saddle point has zero gradient, just like a minimum, but curves upward in some directions and downward in others, rather than upward in every direction. It is not a minimum at all, but it can still slow gradient descent down significantly since the gradient briefly becomes very small there.
Modern optimizers like Adam include mechanisms specifically designed to help push through these low-gradient saddle regions more quickly than plain gradient descent would on its own.

Near a saddle point, the gradient magnitude can shrink dramatically without actually being at a true minimum, which can make training temporarily look like it has stalled even though it has not truly gotten stuck.

Distinguishing a true local minimum from a saddle point by eye on a training loss curve alone can be difficult, the second derivative test from later in this lesson gives a more rigorous way to tell them apart.
6. Local Minima in High Dimensions

A key modern deep learning insight is that in very high dimensional parameter spaces, genuine local minima that are meaningfully worse than the best achievable value turn out to be far rarer than saddle points. For a point to be a true local minimum in high dimensions, the surface must curve upward in every single one of the many available directions simultaneously, an increasingly unlikely coincidence as dimension grows.

This insight reframed how researchers think about deep learning optimization, shifting concern away from getting permanently stuck in a bad minimum and toward simply navigating past slow, flat saddle regions efficiently.

Empirical studies training the same large network from many different random starting points have found that the final loss values achieved are often remarkably close to each other, supporting this theoretical expectation.
This is one of the more surprising, reassuring discoveries to come out of studying deep learning optimization theoretically rather than relying purely on empirical trial and error.
7. Escaping Local Minima

Several practical techniques help an optimizer avoid getting permanently stuck: momentum can carry an optimizer through a shallow local minimum using accumulated velocity, the noise in stochastic gradient descent can nudge a search out of a shallow basin, and random restarts from several different starting points let the best result across multiple attempts be kept.
None of these techniques guarantee finding the true global minimum, they simply improve the odds of finding a good, if not provably best, minimum within a reasonable amount of training time.

Adaptive optimizers like Adam combine several of these ideas together, blending a form of momentum with per-parameter learning rate adjustment specifically to navigate tricky regions of the loss surface more robustly.
Choosing among these escape techniques is rarely an either-or decision, most modern training setups combine several of them together by default.
8. Visualizing Multiple Local Minima

blocks.alt: A function with two local minima
blocks.caption: One is deeper than the other, only the deeper one is the global minimum

blocks.text: A real loss surface for a neural network exists in a space with millions of dimensions, far beyond what any diagram could show directly, this simplified 2D picture only illustrates the basic shape-based intuition.
Even so, low dimensional visualizations like this remain a genuinely useful teaching tool for building the right intuition before working with the full, unvisualizable complexity of a real model.
9. The Second Derivative Test

For a smooth function, a point where the first derivative is zero is a local minimum if the second derivative there is positive, meaning the function curves upward around that point. This directly connects to the Hessian, the multivariable generalization of the second derivative, covered in the calculus module, where a positive definite Hessian at a zero-gradient point confirms a local minimum.

code.content:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
f_expr = x**4 - 4*x**2 + x
first_deriv = sp.diff(f_expr, x)
second_deriv = sp.diff(f_expr, x, 2)
critical_points = sp.solve(first_deriv, x)
for pt in critical_points:
    print(pt, second_deriv.subs(x, pt))   # positive means a local minimum at that point

blocks.text: This same curvature-based reasoning is what the convex-vs-non-convex-functions lesson relies on when describing why a convex bowl shape only ever has the one guaranteed minimum.

When the second derivative test gives exactly 0, the test is inconclusive, and additional information, such as higher order derivatives, is needed to determine whether the point is a minimum, maximum, or something else.
Running this kind of symbolic check with a tool like sympy is far more reliable than eyeballing a plotted curve, especially for functions with several closely spaced critical points.
10. Local Minima and Model Capacity

The number and depth of local minima in a loss surface generally depends on how complex the underlying model is. A model with very few parameters has a simpler, more constrained loss surface with fewer possible local minima, while a model with millions of parameters has an extremely complex surface, though modern research suggests most of those local minima end up being nearly as good as each other in practice.
This is one of several findings that helped explain why very large neural networks, despite having an enormous number of theoretically possible local minima, still train successfully in practice.

This finding is one of the more reassuring, counterintuitive results in deep learning theory, more parameters do not necessarily mean more risk of getting stuck in a bad spot, in some respects it can mean the opposite.

This connects the two seemingly opposite intuitions from earlier sections, more parameters create more theoretical local minima, yet those minima tend to be more uniformly good rather than more dangerous.
11. A Worked Example
Find both local minima of the function f(x) = x to the 4th power minus 4x squared plus x by starting gradient descent from two different points.

code.content:
grad = lambda x: 4*x**3 - 8*x + 1
result_a = gradient_descent_1d(-2.0, 0.01, 500, grad)
result_b = gradient_descent_1d(2.0, 0.01, 500, grad)
print(result_a, f(result_a))
print(result_b, f(result_b))

blocks.text: Comparing the function value at each converged point directly answers which of the two candidate minima is actually the better, lower one for this particular function.
Trying additional starting points beyond just these two would map out the full landscape of local minima this particular function has, confirming whether more than two exist.
12. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming gradient descent always finds the best possible minimum, it only guarantees finding some local minimum on a non-convex surface.
Panicking when training loss plateaus, assuming it always means a bad local minimum, when it may simply be a slow but still improving region, or a saddle point being slowly escaped.
Forgetting that starting point and randomness in initialization can meaningfully change which local minimum a model training run converges to.
Overestimating how big a problem local minima are in modern deep learning, where saddle points are now understood to be the more common practical obstacle.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: tuning a model for a very long time chasing a lower loss, when the remaining gap may reflect an essentially negligible difference between two comparably good local minima.
It is also easy to mistake a temporarily slow-moving training loss for being permanently stuck, when patience and continued training sometimes reveal it was only navigating a difficult saddle region.
13. Practice: Find Local Minima
Run gradient descent on f(x) = sin(x) plus 0.1 times x squared from three different starting points and compare the resulting minima found.

code.content:
import math
grad2 = lambda x: math.cos(x) + 0.2*x
for start in [-5, 0, 5]:
    print(start, gradient_descent_1d(start, 0.1, 500, grad2))

blocks.text: Comparing the three resulting minima found from different starting points directly illustrates the starting-point sensitivity covered in section 4.
Try adjusting the learning rate in this same experiment and observe whether a different rate leads any of the three starting points to a different final minimum than before.
Key Takeaway

A local minimum is lower than every nearby point but not necessarily the best point overall, and gradient descent, which only follows the local slope, can settle into one and stop there. In high dimensional deep learning models, saddle points, not genuine bad local minima, are now understood to be the more common practical obstacle.

The global minima lesson immediately ahead covers the single best possible minimum every optimization process is ultimately hoping to find, and the practical techniques used to search for it despite these local minima and saddle point challenges.

The second derivative test from section 9, and its multivariable Hessian based generalization, give a precise, checkable way to confirm a candidate point is genuinely a local minimum rather than a saddle point or something else entirely.

Model capacity, from section 10, interacts directly with this whole picture, larger models tend to have flatter, more forgiving loss landscapes where most local minima end up being nearly as good as each other.

Recognizing whether slow training progress reflects a genuine problem or simply a difficult saddle region being navigated is one of the most valuable diagnostic instincts to develop when training real models.
